title: Jev vs GPT Decisions: ECG Classification on CODE Test – Felipe Dias
text: Can System-One AI Models Classify ECG Images? ECG AI Experiments Can two general-purpose decision models identify ECG abnormalities from images? A zero-shot evaluation on CODE Test using AUROC and probability calibration. Author Felipe Meneguitti Dias Published October 15, 2026 I wanted to try something simple: what happens when we show an ECG to an AI model that was not built specifically for ECG interpretation? There are already good models trained on ECG signals. Here, I was curious about two newer systems that take an image and return a structured decision. Would they recognize common ECG findings? And when they say YES or NO, how meaningful are their probabilities? This is an exploratory experiment, not a clinical diagnostic tool. The experimental inputs and analysis scripts are retained in private research repositories. The models I tested Jev 1.14.0 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions , accessed through OpenAI’s Decisions API . Both belong to a category I refer to here as System-One AI : models designed to make direct, structured decisions instead of writing long explanations. The name is an analogy, not a claim about how these networks think. Both APIs can look at an image and answer questions such as “Is atrial fibrillation present?” They return YES or NO and a probability for each answer. That gives us more to evaluate than a binary prediction alone. The ECGs I used 827 exams from the CODE Test dataset . The original recordings are digital signals, but the models only saw images of twelve-lead ECGs. The images were created using ecg-plot , in the same Sangha-style layout used in an earlier ECG image study. The rendered images and labels are retained as research materials. We evaluated six findings: Label Finding Positive exams 1dAVb First-degree AV block 28 RBBB Right bundle branch block 34 LBBB Left bundle branch block 30 SB Sinus bradycardia 16 AF Atrial fibrillation 13 ST Sinus tachycardia 37 This is a multilabel task. One ECG can have more than one finding. And an ECG with none of these six labels is not necessarily normal. I resized each image once, keeping its aspect ratio, and sent the same PNG to both APIs. Neither received the raw signals, clinical history, or correct labels. The resizing itself may hide small details, which is one limitation of this setup. I did not give the models a list of cardiology rules. For each finding, I asked: Assess the 12-lead ECG image in `ecg_image`. Is {condition} present? Evaluate this finding independently of other diagnoses. YES: {condition} is present NO: {condition} is absent For atrial fibrillation, {condition} becomes Atrial fibrillation . GPT Decisions received the equivalent independent questions, using its own API format. The complete request payloads and inference scripts are retained privately for reproducibility. One example illustrates why the probabilities matter. On ECG ecg_0 , both models correctly answered NO for LBBB. But Jev assigned 0.49 to YES, while GPT Decisions assigned 0.00 . The decisions matched, but the models expressed very different levels of certainty. These are probabilities returned by the APIs, not validated estimates of clinical risk. How I measured performance Jev returned predictions for all 827 images. GPT Decisions succeeded on 826 and failed on ecg_818 . I excluded that image from both models so the comparison uses exactly the same 826 ECGs . I focused on two questions. Discrimination: does a model give higher scores to ECGs that truly have a finding? I measured this with the area under the ROC curve ( AUROC ). A value near 0.5 indicates little ability to rank positive and negative cases. A value near 1.0 is much better. Calibration: when a model says 70%, does the finding actually occur about 70% of the time among exams with that predicted probability? A model can rank cases well while reporting poor probabilities. I also calculated the Brier Score , the average squared difference between the predicted probability and the true label. Lower is better. Brier reflects both probability calibration and discrimination, so it should not be treated as a pure calibration measure. Results Figure 1. Top: ROC curves for the six findings. The values marked AUROC show the area under each curve. Bottom: predicted versus observed probabilities, with score histograms. The dashed line marks perfect calibration. Shaded regions show pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals from 1,000 stratified resamples. Calibration curves use shape-preserving PCHIP interpolation between observed bin means, without extrapolating beyond the data. The interpolation changes the display, not the model predictions. Finding Jev AUROC GPT AUROC Jev Brier ↓ GPT Brier ↓ 1dAVb 0.453 0.457 0.135 0.066 RBBB 0.601 0.805 0.137 0.039 LBBB 0.976 0.953 0.173 0.025 SB 0.730 0.789 0.158 0.021 AF 0.613 0.697 0.185 0.022 ST 0.778 0.966 0.228 0.026 GPT Decisions had a higher macro-AUROC ( 0.778 versus 0.692 ) and a lower mean Brier Score ( 0.033 versus 0.169 ). Jev did particularly well on LBBB, with an AUROC of 0.976 . The differences across findings are striking. For some diagnoses, the models could rank exams fairly well. For others, especially first-degree AV block, they struggled. I would not draw strong clinical conclusions from these numbers. Only 13 exams were positive for AF and 16 for SB. That makes calibration estimates especially uncertain. The shaded intervals describe uncertainty within this sample, not a formal statistical test of which model is better. A prevalence-only baseline would also be useful when interpreting Brier Scores. How does this compare with an ECG-specific model? Sangha et al. (2022) trained a model specifically to classify ECG images. Their paper reports results on the cardiologist-validated CODE Test set of 827 ECGs , which is the same cohort used in this experiment. Below are the AUROCs for all six diagnoses, taken directly from Table 1 of their paper. Finding Sangha image model AUROC (95% CI) First-degree AV block (1dAVb) 0.995 (0.991–0.999) Right bundle branch block (RBBB) 0.995 (0.992–0.999) Left bundle branch block (LBBB) 1.000 (1.000–1.000) Sinus bradycardia (SB) 0.997 (0.994–1.000) Atrial fibrillation (AF) 0.997 (0.993–1.000) Sinus tachycardia (ST) 0.998 (0.996–1.000) Source: Sangha et al., Nature Communications (2022), Table 1, image-based model, cardiologist-validated test set (N = 827). The reported class-weighted mean AUROC was 0.997 (95% CI 0.994–1.000). These are impressive results for a model trained specifically on ECG images. They also give useful context for our exploratory experiment. The published numbers and our API results are not an exactly matched head-to-head evaluation: our paired analysis uses 826 ECGs, and image preprocessing and model development differ. See the original study for the full evaluation. Where to go next The CODE Test is a useful starting point, but it is small for this kind of evaluation. I would like to repeat the experiment on larger and more varied collections. PTB-XL contains 21,799 ECG recordings and many diagnostic labels. It could help us see whether these findings hold with more exams and different conditions. The George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2024 is another interesting direction because it includes ECG images with different layouts and visual artifacts. That would test something the clean CODE renderings cannot: how robust the models are to the kinds of images we see outside a controlled benchmark. Update, October 2026: We have now completed the larger experiment. Read the PTB-XL follow-up with 21,796 paired ECGs, AUROC, calibration and F1-score . The PhysioNet Challenge 2024 remains a separate evaluation protocol. Final thoughts Both models could read an ECG image and return structured answers. That alone is interesting, but it does not mean they can interpret ECGs reliably. GPT Decisions generally performed better in this experiment, while Jev showed strong discrimination for LBBB. More importantly, the experiment reminded me that making a decision, ranking cases correctly, and assigning useful probabilities are different abilities . title: Jev vs GPT Decisions on PTB-XL: ECG Classification and Calibration – Felipe Dias
text: What Happens When Decision Models Read 21,799 ECG Images? ECG AI Experiments A follow-up to CODE Test: Jev and GPT Decisions on PTB-XL, with discrimination, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1. Author Felipe Meneguitti Dias Published October 16, 2026 In my first experiment , I gave Jev and GPT Decisions 827 ECG images from CODE Test. The results were interesting, but the dataset was small, and some diagnoses had very few positive examples. I ended that post by suggesting a larger test with PTB-XL. This is that follow-up. This time, I wanted to see what happens when we ask the same kind of models to read 21,799 ECGs , with five broader diagnostic categories. I also wanted to look beyond AUROC: what happens when we actually turn a probability into a YES or NO? The ECGs and the models I used PTB-XL version 1.0.3 , a publicly available collection of 12-lead ECG recordings. Instead of sending raw signals, I used the clean images already rendered by GenECG . The experiment records the image source and SHA-256 checksum for each examination. I tested Jev 1.14.0 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions . Both received the same ECG PNG and five independent YES/NO questions. No signal samples, patient history or reference labels were included in the requests. The shared instructions tell the models that the task is multilabel, that MI includes patterns of previous infarction, and that ST-T changes can coexist with other findings. For example, the MI question was: You are evaluating a standard 12-lead ECG image. Assess five PTB-XL diagnostic superclasses independently. This is a MULTILABEL task. Question: Is MI present? Myocardial infarction pattern: pathological Q waves, QRS or ST-T changes suggestive of myocardial infarction, including prior infarction. This does not mean acute STEMI specifically. Return YES or NO. The same diagnostic definitions were used in both API requests. Each model returned a binary answer and a probability for YES. How I evaluated the answers Of the 21,799 ECGs, 21,796 had complete, valid responses from both models . Three failed API calls were excluded from both sides. All metrics below use the same paired set. I measured AUROC for discrimination and examined calibration by comparing predicted probabilities with observed frequencies. I also calculated the Brier Score . For the binary decisions, I report sensitivity (Se), specificity (Spe), precision (positive predictive value), and F1-score. I used two approaches: Fixed threshold 0.5: classify as positive when the reported YES probability is at least 0.5. F1-optimized threshold: use nine of PTB-XL’s ten predefined folds to select a threshold that maximizes F1, then apply it to the held-out fold. Repeat across folds and pool the held-out predictions. This is an out-of-fold threshold evaluation, not a threshold chosen on the cases being scored. Threshold optimization uses PTB-XL reference labels. It is therefore a form of supervised adaptation, even though the underlying model weights were not fine-tuned. Discrimination and calibration Figure 1. Top: empirical ROC curves for the five superclasses. Bottom: predicted versus observed probabilities, with score histograms. The dashed diagonal marks chance discrimination or perfect calibration. Shaded regions and AUROC intervals use 300 paired patient-cluster bootstrap resamples. Calibration uses the same quantile-binning and shape-preserving PCHIP interpolation as the CODE Test figure, within observed support only. Both figures are generated by the same Python rendering function, adapted to five or six classes. The probabilities are not recalibrated. Class Jev AUROC (95% CI) GPT AUROC (95% CI) NORM 0.702 (0.695–0.709) 0.677 (0.671–0.682) MI 0.669 (0.659–0.678) 0.724 (0.715–0.731) STTC 0.465 (0.456–0.475) 0.655 (0.646–0.664) CD 0.535 (0.525–0.545) 0.706 (0.697–0.715) HYP 0.697 (0.686–0.709) 0.677 (0.668–0.689) The most striking result is the uneven performance. Jev ranked normal ECGs and hypertrophy slightly better. GPT Decisions ranked infarction patterns, ST-T changes and conduction disturbances better. Neither performed consistently well across all five classes. Jev’s STTC AUROC of 0.465 is particularly concerning. Its scores did not meaningfully separate positive from negative cases in the expected direction. What happens at a threshold of 0.5? Class Model Se Spe Precision F1 @ 0.5 F1 optimized* NORM Jev 0.000 1.000 0.000 0.000 0.667 GPT 0.004 1.000 0.952 0.008 0.608 MI Jev 0.785 0.407 0.307 0.441 0.462 GPT 0.180 0.951 0.551 0.271 0.507 STTC Jev 0.997 0.000 0.234 0.379 0.380 GPT 0.980 0.081 0.246 0.394 0.426 CD Jev 0.012 0.997 0.513 0.024 0.367 GPT 0.081 0.987 0.647 0.144 0.474 HYP Jev 0.122 0.972 0.379 0.184 0.323 GPT 0.330 0.855 0.239 0.278 0.297 Macro F1 Jev 0.206 0.440 GPT 0.219 0.462 The optimized F1 column pools predictions from ten held-out folds, with each fold’s threshold selected from the other nine folds. Se, Spe and precision in this table are for the fixed 0.5 threshold. The threshold matters a lot. At 0.5, Jev almost never identifies NORM or CD, even though its AUROC for NORM is above 0.7. The probabilities contain some ranking information, but a generic 0.5 cutoff is a poor decision rule. Selecting thresholds from separate folds improves macro F1 from 0.206 to 0.440 for Jev and from 0.219 to 0.462 for GPT Decisions. This should not be confused with an improvement in the underlying model or with prospective clinical validation. How does this compare with my PhysioNet Challenge 2024 model? In 2024, our AIMED team developed an ECG-specific ConvNeXt model for the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge. The approach combined ImageNet pretraining, ECG-domain transfer learning and explicit fine-tuning on ECG data. It won the ECG image-classification task. Our Computing in Cardiology 2024 paper reported a macro F1-score of 0.817 on the Challenge’s hidden evaluation. Internal five-fold validation reported 0.698 ± 0.022 . Evaluation Macro F1 Jev, PTB-XL GenECG, threshold 0.5 0.206 GPT Decisions, PTB-XL GenECG, threshold 0.5 0.219 Jev, PTB-XL GenECG, out-of-fold threshold 0.440 GPT Decisions, PTB-XL GenECG, out-of-fold threshold 0.462 AIMED ConvNeXt, Challenge 2024 hidden evaluation 0.817 These scores are not directly comparable. The Challenge used a different set of diagnostic classes, a hidden evaluation set and a different image-generation and acquisition protocol. Its 0.817 result is useful context for a specialist ECG-image model, not a head-to-head benchmark on these 21,796 images. There is another important distinction. My ConvNeXt model was explicitly trained and fine-tuned for ECG classification. Jev and GPT Decisions were not explicitly fine-tuned on PTB-XL for this experiment. Their broader pretraining data are not fully disclosed, so we cannot rule out previous exposure to ECG material or PTB-XL examples. The threshold-optimized results also use labeled PTB-XL examples to select thresholds. These differences are limitations, not evidence of an intrinsic model advantage. What I take from this The larger dataset changes the picture from the first CODE Test experiment. Both APIs reliably produced structured outputs, but that alone did not make their ECG interpretations dependable. Some classes were ranked reasonably well, while others showed weak discrimination or highly unsuitable probability thresholds. For me, the most useful finding is the gap between ranking an ECG, reporting a probability, and making a binary clinical decision . They are related tasks, but not interchangeable. The next experiment should test the models on different ECG acquisition conditions and use an independent dataset for selecting thresholds before evaluating new cases. Reproducibility and references Both articles use one shared figure renderer, with identical fonts, colors, empirical ROC steps, calibration panels, histograms and uncertainty-band conventions. PTB-XL resamples patients as clusters to account for repeated ECGs. CODE Test uses class-stratified resampling. The underlying inference scripts and individual results are retained privately. title: PhysioNet Challenge 2024 | Felipe Meneguitti Dias
text: ← All projects ECG image classification · 2024 PhysioNet Challenge 2024 Heart Institute (InCor), Hospital das Clínicas, University of São Paulo Medical School ECG image research at InCor When the 2024 topic was announced, I was already studying ECG image classification during my PhD at the University of São Paulo and InCor. Many hospital ECGs were stored as images, while most models expected time-series signals. That mismatch was central to my research. I led AIMED in the challenge. We used what I had already tested during my PhD to choose the training strategy. The organizers then evaluated our code on unseen data. We finished first in classification. Award presentation at Computing in Cardiology 2024 in Karlsruhe, Germany. From left to right: Matthew Reyna, Felipe Dias, Marco Antônio Gutierrez and Gari Clifford. Photo: SBIS. What is the PhysioNet Challenge? Pretraining First place: team AIMED News coverage What is the PhysioNet Challenge? The PhysioNet Challenge is an annual research competition organized by PhysioNet and Computing in Cardiology since 2000. Each year, teams work on the same clinical or physiological problem. The organizers provide the data and evaluation rules, test the algorithms and make the code available so other researchers can study and reproduce the methods. The 2024 problem: ECGs on paper The 2024 topic was Digitization and Classification of ECG Images. There were two tasks, with separate awards. Teams could enter either task or both: Digitization Reconstruct the lead time series from an image of the ECG. Classification Identify ECG categories from the image, either directly or using reconstructed signals. Teams submitted their code, and the organizers ran the training and evaluation. Each team selected a final version for testing on hidden data. We focused on classifying the images directly. Why we chose to classify the image Digitizing an ECG means recovering the signal from the image. It involves separating each lead from the grid, recovering the time and amplitude scales, and dealing with overlapping traces, shadows, perspective and noise. Errors can carry through to the classifier that uses the reconstructed signal. I had already tested CNNs for ECG image classification, so we decided to focus on that task. The model analyzes the image directly, without first reconstructing the signal. Doctoral experiments During my PhD, I used synthetic images generated from public ECG signals and real ECGs from InCor's outpatient and emergency departments. I compared ConvNeXt, EfficientNet-B3, ResNet50, ViT and Swin Transformer, and tested different ways to train them. I tested data augmentation and different image resolutions. I compared ImageNet initialization, ECG pretraining and the combination of both. I tested adding age and sex, and using a loss function that combined BCE and MCC. I ran ablation studies to assess individual choices, and tested the models on photographed and scanned ECGs. Our challenge entry built on some of these experiments. The training strategy we submitted is outlined below. Pretraining We started with ImageNet weights, but ECGs look very different from the photographs in that dataset. Before fine-tuning for the challenge, we trained the network on synthetic and real ECG images. In my thesis, I also tested random initialization followed by ECG-only pretraining. Macro F1 was lower than with ImageNet initialization. Combining ImageNet initialization with ECG pretraining gave the best result among the three configurations below. We used that combination in the competition. Initialization and pretraining Macro F1 ImageNet, without ECG-specific pretraining 0.737 Random weights + ECG pretraining 0.565 ImageNet + ECG pretraining 0.759 Thesis ablation results from 10-fold cross-validation on InCor-EMG. The PhysioNet Challenge evaluation appears in the results section. Doctoral thesis, including Appendix A on the challenge . Published method Our paper, Image-Based Electrocardiogram Classification Using Pre-trained ConvNext, describes the training strategy we used in the challenge: AIMED’s final method, reproduced from Figure 1 of the CinC 2024 paper. ImageNet We started with a ConvNeXt pretrained on general images. CODE15 and InCor-AMB We adapted the network to synthetic images generated with ECG-Image-Kit and real outpatient ECGs. InCor-EMG We performed an additional fine-tuning stage on emergency ECG images. PTB-XL We fine-tuned for the 11 challenge categories using 5-fold cross-validation and combined the five models into an ensemble. We used grayscale images at 224 × 224 resolution for pretraining and 384 × 384 for final fine-tuning. Training included data augmentation, AdamW, class-weighted BCE and early stopping. The 11 categories covered normal ECGs, infarction, ST/T changes, conduction disturbances and arrhythmias. We left CINC21 out of pretraining because it contains PTB-XL. We also reduced cross-validation from 10 to 5 folds to stay within the challenge computing limits. First place: team AIMED AIMED finished first among the 16 official classification entries, with a macro F1 of 0.817. The extended evaluation also tested phone photos, stained or damaged paper and monitor screenshots. Our average score across the eight scenarios was 0.733. Scores were lower on photographs. title: Gorgona | Felipe Meneguitti Dias
text: ← Todos os projetos ECGs de UPAs · InCor · 2026 Gorgona Classificação de ECGs integrada ao atendimento de urgência Instituto do Coração (InCor), Hospital das Clínicas da Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo Objetivo Quando um ECG feito na UPA sugere infarto agudo do miocárdio, o Gorgona avisa a equipe de regulação pelo Telegram. O exame também segue para a telemedicina. A ideia é antecipar o aviso para que a equipe médica avalie o paciente e decida a conduta. O que fiz Além de liderar o projeto, fiz a integração inicial entre o modelo, o programa Windows, o servidor do InCor, o painel e o Telegram. Trabalhei junto à equipe clínica, responsável pelo protocolo de atendimento e pela avaliação dos exames. Fluxo proposto com IA. Figura original do projeto. 2 min entre o ECG e o alerta neste caso 41 min antes do primeiro laudo Objetivo Fluxo anterior e fluxo com IA Servidor e plataforma online Estudo de caso Local da implantação Implantamos o sistema na UPA Rodrigo Argolo, no bairro de Tancredo Neves, em Salvador. Os ECGs são feitos na UPA e analisados no servidor do InCor. Localização aproximada da UPA. Rua Pernambuco, s/n, Salvador. CNES 7033850. Mapa: © OpenStreetMap contributors. Endereço: CNES/DATASUS. Coordenadas: SaúdeNoPais. Como funciona Fluxo anterior A equipe enviava o ECG à telemedicina manualmente. Depois do laudo e da avaliação médica, podia acionar a regulação pelo Telegram. Quando a suspeita clínica era forte, o médico da UPA também podia contatar o grupo diretamente. Com o Gorgona O programa acompanha a pasta de exames e envia os novos arquivos ao InCor para classificação. Quando a probabilidade da classe Corrente de Lesão passa de 50%, o sistema avisa o grupo de regulação pelo Telegram. Fluxo anterior e fluxo com IA. Diagramas originais do projeto. Cada instalação tem sua própria credencial. Pelo menu na bandeja do Windows, a equipe pode configurar o programa, reiniciá-lo ou reenviar arquivos. ECG-IA Client 1.6.66 · Windows ECG-IA Client · Menu na bandeja do Windows Servidor e plataforma online Uma API em FastAPI recebe o exame, lê os metadados e converte o traçado em imagem quando necessário. As classes e probabilidades ficam em SQLite. O painel mostra os resultados e o estado dos clientes, e a integração com o Telegram envia os alertas. Arquitetura do sistema. Proteção de dados e LGPD O cliente permite anonimizar os arquivos no computador da UPA antes do envio. A transmissão usa HTTPS, com credenciais por instalação e perfis de acesso. Esses recursos, isoladamente, não comprovam conformidade integral com a LGPD. O painel permite filtrar resultados por unidade, período, status e classe. Painel do Gorgona: filtros e resultados de classificação. Resultados e avaliação Estudo de caso O caso é de um atendimento em 20 de maio de 2026, na UPA Rodrigo Argolo. O paciente deu entrada às 18h52 e fez dois ECGs. Cada exame gerou um alerta 2 minutos depois. A chegada ao centro de referência foi registrada às 20h44. Horários do estudo de caso, a partir do primeiro ECG. Admissão às 18h52. A identificação do paciente foi retirada. Evento Primeiro ECG Segundo ECG Realização do ECG 19h15 19h37 Alerta da IA 19h17 19h39 Chegada à telemedicina 19h21 19h39 Emissão do laudo 19h58 20h04 Do exame ao alerta 2 min 2 min Antecedência em relação ao laudo 41 min 25 min O primeiro alerta chegou 4 minutos antes de o exame entrar na telemedicina. Os dois avisos antecederam os laudos em 41 e 25 minutos. A regulação recebeu a informação mais cedo, mas esse caso isolado não permite concluir que a IA reduziu o tempo de tratamento ou melhorou o desfecho. Modelo de classificação O Gorgona usa como base o modelo da AIMED, equipe que liderei no PhysioNet Challenge 2024. Ficamos em primeiro lugar em classificação. O artigo do CinC 2024 descreve o pré-treinamento com ECGs e o ensemble ConvNeXt. Na minha tese, detalho os bancos de imagens, os experimentos e a avaliação clínica. O classificador reúne modelos ConvNeXt para identificar 12 categorias. No estudo com 18.519 ECGs de 14.402 pacientes, anotados por 19 cardiologistas, o macro F1 no teste reservado foi de 0,807 (IC 95%: 0,788 a 0,825). title: PhysioNet Challenge 2024 | Felipe Meneguitti Dias
text: ← Todos os projetos Classificação de imagens de ECG · 2024 PhysioNet Challenge 2024 Instituto do Coração (InCor), Hospital das Clínicas da Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo Pesquisa com imagens de ECG no InCor Quando o tema de 2024 foi anunciado, eu já estudava a classificação de ECGs por imagem no doutorado, na USP e no InCor. Muitos exames do hospital estavam armazenados como imagens, mas os modelos geralmente recebiam o sinal em série temporal. Minha pesquisa partia dessa diferença. Na AIMED, equipe que liderei, aproveitamos o que eu já havia testado no doutorado para definir o treinamento. Os organizadores avaliaram nosso código com dados que não conhecíamos. Ficamos em primeiro lugar em classificação. Entrega do prêmio no Computing in Cardiology 2024, em Karlsruhe, Alemanha. Da esquerda para a direita: Matthew Reyna, Felipe Dias, Marco Antônio Gutierrez e Gari Clifford. Foto: SBIS. O que é o PhysioNet Challenge? Pré-treinamento Primeiro lugar: equipe AIMED Notícias sobre a premiação O que é o PhysioNet Challenge? O PhysioNet Challenge é uma competição anual de pesquisa, organizada pelo PhysioNet e pelo Computing in Cardiology desde 2000. A cada ano, as equipes trabalham com um mesmo problema clínico ou fisiológico. Os organizadores fornecem os dados e as regras de avaliação, testam os algoritmos e disponibilizam o código para que outros pesquisadores possam estudar e reproduzir os métodos. O problema de 2024: ECGs em papel Em 2024, o tema foi Digitization and Classification of ECG Images. Havia duas tarefas, com premiações separadas. As equipes podiam participar de uma delas ou das duas: Digitalização Reconstruir as séries temporais das derivações a partir da imagem do exame. Classificação Identificar categorias do ECG a partir da imagem, diretamente ou usando sinais reconstruídos. As equipes enviavam o código, e os organizadores executavam o treinamento e a avaliação. Cada equipe escolhia uma versão final para o teste com dados ocultos. Concentramos nosso trabalho na classificação direta das imagens. Por que escolhemos classificar a imagem Digitalizar um ECG significa recuperar o sinal a partir da imagem. Isso exige separar cada derivação da grade, recuperar as escalas de tempo e amplitude e lidar com traçados sobrepostos, sombras, perspectiva e ruído. Um erro nessa etapa pode se propagar para o classificador que usa o sinal reconstruído. Eu já tinha testado CNNs para classificar imagens de ECG, então decidimos concentrar o esforço nessa tarefa. O modelo analisa a imagem diretamente, sem uma etapa de reconstrução do sinal. Experimentos do doutorado No doutorado, usei imagens sintéticas geradas a partir de sinais públicos e ECGs reais do ambulatório e da emergência do InCor. Comparei ConvNeXt, EfficientNet-B3, ResNet50, ViT e Swin Transformer e testei diferentes formas de treinar essas redes. Testei aumento de dados e diferentes resoluções de imagem. Comparei a inicialização com ImageNet, o pré-treinamento com ECGs e a combinação dos dois. Experimentei incluir idade e sexo e usar uma função de perda que combinava BCE e MCC. Fiz estudos de ablação para avaliar cada escolha e testes com exames fotografados e escaneados. O desafio aproveitou parte desses experimentos. O treinamento que submetemos está descrito abaixo. Pré-treinamento Partimos dos pesos do ImageNet, mas um ECG é bem diferente das fotografias desse banco. Antes do ajuste para o desafio, treinamos a rede com imagens de ECG sintéticas e reais. Na tese, também testei a inicialização com pesos aleatórios seguida de pré-treinamento só com ECGs. O macro F1 foi menor do que com a inicialização pelo ImageNet. A combinação de ImageNet e pré-treinamento com ECGs teve o melhor resultado entre as três configurações abaixo, e foi a que usamos na competição. Inicialização e pré-treinamento Macro F1 ImageNet, sem pré-treinamento específico em ECG 0,737 Pesos aleatórios + pré-treinamento em ECG 0,565 ImageNet + pré-treinamento em ECG 0,759 Resultados de ablação da tese, com validação cruzada de 10 folds no InCor-EMG. A avaliação do PhysioNet Challenge aparece na seção de resultados. Tese de doutorado, incluindo o Apêndice A sobre o desafio . Método publicado No artigo Image-Based Electrocardiogram Classification Using Pre-trained ConvNext, mostramos o treinamento usado no desafio: Metodologia final da AIMED, reproduzida da Figura 1 do artigo do CinC 2024. ImageNet Começamos com uma ConvNeXt pré-treinada em imagens gerais. CODE15 e InCor-AMB Adaptamos a rede a imagens sintéticas geradas com ECG-Image-Kit e a ECGs reais do ambulatório. InCor-EMG Fizemos um ajuste adicional com imagens da emergência. PTB-XL Ajustamos para as 11 categorias do desafio com validação cruzada de 5 folds e reunimos os cinco modelos em um ensemble. Usamos imagens em tons de cinza, com resolução de 224 × 224 no pré-treinamento e 384 × 384 no ajuste final. O treinamento incluiu aumento de dados, AdamW, BCE ponderada por classe e early stopping. As 11 categorias abrangiam normalidade, infarto, alterações de ST/T, distúrbios de condução e arritmias. Retiramos o CINC21 do pré-treinamento porque ele contém o PTB-XL. Também passamos de 10 para 5 folds de validação cruzada para respeitar os limites computacionais do desafio. Primeiro lugar: equipe AIMED A AIMED ficou em primeiro lugar entre as 16 entradas oficiais da tarefa de classificação, com macro F1 de 0,817. Estes foram os três primeiros resultados publicados pelos organizadores: Colocação Equipe Macro F1 do ranking 1º AIMED 0,817 2º Inventec AIC 0,742 3º BAPORLab 0,730 Consultar a tabela oficial de classificação O ranking foi calculado com imagens de ECGs em papel escaneadas em cores e em preto e branco. A avaliação estendida também incluiu fotos de celular, papel manchado ou deteriorado e capturas de tela. Nos oito cenários, nossa média foi 0,733. O desempenho caiu nas fotografias. Certificado de primeiro lugar em classificação, equipe AIMED. Karlsruhe, 11 de setembro de 2024. Equipe Liderei a AIMED e fui o primeiro autor do artigo. O trabalho foi feito com Estela Ribeiro, Quenaz B. Soares, José E. Krieger e Marco A. Gutierrez, no Laboratório de Informática Biomédica do InCor. title: RPMS | Felipe Meneguitti Dias
text: ← Todos os projetos Monitoramento remoto · InCor RPMS Remote Patient Monitoring System Instituto do Coração (InCor), Hospital das Clínicas da Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo Objetivo O RPMS usa relógios e um aplicativo para acompanhar medidas fisiológicas fora do hospital. O celular processa os sinais e envia os resultados a um painel que a equipe médica pode consultar. O que fiz Trabalhei com os relógios protótipos, ajudei a definir os protocolos de coleta e organizei os dados. Com a equipe, desenvolvi o pré-processamento dos sinais de fotopletismografia (PPG) e os algoritmos usados no projeto. Como funciona Relógio, aplicativo e painel médico. Figura 1 de Moreno, Dias et al., SIoT (2022). O relógio envia o PPG ao aplicativo Android por Bluetooth Low Energy. O celular processa o sinal, estima pressão arterial e frequência cardíaca e envia os resultados por MQTT ao servidor ThingsBoard. O painel permite acompanhar as medidas de cada paciente ao longo do tempo. Resultados e avaliação Na arquitetura publicada em 2022, o aplicativo mantinha o histórico das medidas no celular e enviava ao servidor as estimativas de pressão sistólica, diastólica e frequência cardíaca. Aplicativo Android: coleta de PPG, medidas e histórico. Figura 3, SIoT 2022. Painel ThingsBoard com as medidas recebidas. Figura 4, SIoT 2022. Protocolo e processamento do sinal No protocolo de 2022, cada voluntário descansava por 10 minutos. Depois, fazia três coletas de um minuto de PPG, intercaladas com medidas de pressão por manguito.
